newsitem.title: CANADA: Precision says Kenting offer still high.
newsitem.headline: Precision says Kenting offer still high.

text.p: Precision Drilling Corp, which late Wednesday confirmed its intention to make a takeover bid for rival Kenting Energy Services Inc, believes its offer still puts top value on the firm's assets, Precision chief financial officer Dale Tremblay said on Thursday.
"I think the bid is pretty high," Tremblay said in a phone interview. "Why would I pay more when there is no other offer?"

Precision said it would offer C$3.50 cash plus a 10th of a Precision share for each Kenting share, the same amount as its earlier announcement. The bid now accounts for extra assets Kenting is acquiring through a merger with Lynx Energy Services Corp.
A successful deal would give Precision a market share of almost 40 percent in Canada's red-hot oil and gas drilling business.
If the price of Precision shares reached C$70, the bid would be valued at C$10.50 per Kenting share, a total of about C$500 million.
However, shares of Precision have fallen over C$11 since its first bid announcement was made in early February.
At Thursday's Precision share price of C$55.50 -- down C$2.50 on the day -- its bid would be valued at C$9, far below Kenting's current price of C$9.95.
Under Precision's offer, the cash portion of the deal would be boosted to C$5 should its stock price dip below C$50.

Tremblay said all moves made by his firm so far in the process were aimed at convincing Kenting to eventually view the bid as a friendly one and allow it to be a permitted offer under Kenting's shareholder rights plan.
He said he expected no other bids to surface.
Kenting has retained ScotiaMcLeod Inc as financial adviser in its quest for a higher offer.

The complex takeover battle began just after Kenting was spun off from transport conglomerate Trimac Ltd in early February. Precision announced its advance the next business day, before Kenting began trading as a stand-alone firm.
Moments after Precision went public with its offer, Kenting said it planned to merge with Lynx, a smaller drilling firm that counted Precision as a major shareholder.
Precision chief executive Hank Swartout said after the flurry of deal announcements that he welcomed the Kenting/Lynx merger and went back to the drawing board to rig up a plan to absorb both.
Tremblay said the Kenting/Lynx merger placed a pricetag of C$3.5 million each on the Lynx drilling rigs, ignoring the value of other assets acquired.

Precision, however, would value the merged entity at C$4.9 million for each of its 97 rigs -- assuming the top Precision share price and again ignoring other businesses and assets, he said, stressing that the rigs were the reason for the offer.
Tremblay said the acquisition was necessary to keep its shareholders happy with stock price growth and stave off being taken over itself, possibly by a large U.S.-based drilling firm.
